pages.title: Things to Do While You Wait

sections.title: Call your Mom - added June 5th
sections.body:
There is a kind of call you owe before you know you owe it. It sits there in the back room of the mind, behind the bills and the small hungers and the bright little emergencies that have been trained to bark first.

Call because there was a time when your voice was the whole weather of her day, and now she gets it in scraps, compressed between errands, interrupted by all the busy machinery you have mistaken for a life.

She will answer in the tone she uses when she is trying not to sound too pleased. Mothers are proud in that way. They learn to take less than they want and call it plenty. She may ask whether you ate or how work was. She may tell you some small, wandering thing about a neighbor, a cousin, the price of fruit, the strange sound the washing machine made this morning.

The point of the call is not the information. The point is the line itself, warm and ordinary, stretched across all the rooms and years between you. Let her talk. Let the little details come, they are not little to her. They are the beads she has been carrying around all day, waiting for a string.

Ask one real question. Ask what she had for lunch. Ask whether she slept well. Ask what has been making her laugh lately. Ask if she has been thinking about anything from when you were small.

Then listen.

You may find, after a minute, that the call changes shape. It stops being a duty and becomes a place you can stand in.

And when she asks about you, tell her one true thing. Tell her you have been tired. The type of tired that sits in your bones and holds you down in the morning. Tell her something good that happened and let her enjoy it without brushing it away. A mother’s joy is one of the few clean fuels left.

Stay on the line a little longer than habit allows. Let there be a silence that does not frighten you. Let her fill it, or do not fill it. Sometimes love is only two people breathing at opposite ends of the wire, silently remembering good times.

Before you hang up, say something plain. “I’m glad I called.” “I was thinking about you.” “I love you.” Say it without comedy, without an escape hatch, without making it smaller so it will not embarrass you.

Afterward, the room may feel different, something small will have been put back where it belongs. A small human repair made while the world was busy trying to sell you something louder.

sections.title: Walk without your phone - added June 5th
sections.body:
Put your phone down on the nearest table then go outside.

At first, you may feel foolish. That is a useful feeling. It tells you how much of your life has been arranged around the idea that you must always be reachable, always available, always carrying the small black door through which the world can enter and ask for more.

The first few minutes may feel empty. Your hand may go to the pocket where the phone usually rides. It will find nothing there, and for a second you may feel a small animal panic. Let the panic spend itself, it has been fed too often.

Look at the houses, the trees, the cracks in the sidewalk. Notice the dull, private labor of ordinary things. A fence leaning slightly out of true. A sprinkler ticking in a bad rhythm. A dog making a grave decision behind a window. The sky, which has been there all day, receiving no credit.

There is a strange mercy in being unavailable. No one can send you a little red number or slide a worry into your palm. No machine can tell you what to want for the next thirty seconds. The world becomes larger because it stops being addressed directly to you.

You may begin to hear things. Tires moving over pavement. Leaves rubbing together. Someone closing a gate. A bird with no talent for melody trying anyway. These are not notifications, they do not require a response.

Let your mind wander where it wants. It may go to work. It may go to money. It may go to some old mistake you thought you had finally lost. Let it go there, then let it move on. A mind, when it is not being whipped from post to post, often knows how to settle itself.

Walk far enough that the urge to check fades into boredom, and far enough past boredom that something quieter appears. You may remember a person you need to call, the answer to a problem you were trying too hard to solve. Or nothing may happen at all, which is also a kind of medicine.

When you come back, the phone will still be waiting. You will return to it from a different place, even if you only walked around the block.

You will have done one clean thing. You gave the world a chance to be itself. You gave yourself the same chance.

sections.title: Can I end a session early?
sections.body: No. Luddite is designed around commitment. Once a session starts, the lock should feel real.

sections.title: What should I do during a session?
sections.body: Do something physical, social, useful, or quiet. Walk, clean, read, cook, stretch, or talk to someone nearby.

sections.title: Why does this app exist?
sections.body: Luddite helps you create a short period where your phone is no longer the easiest option.
